title: Go-to-market
note: Launch playbooks ordered by motion: price and buyer pick the motion, then beachhead, positioning, channel, economics and proof. Fees, programs and benchmarks are dated Nov 2026; refresh yearly.

concepts.s: What one customer pays and who signs the check decide your go-to-market motion; product type is only the branch underneath.

x.b:
Christoph Janz's ladder for a $100M business: about 1,000 customers at $100k a year, 10,000 at $10k, 100,000 at $1k, or 1 million at $100. The price sets how much you can spend to win each customer, and that budget picks the channel.

  • Self-serve consumer: no salesperson; apps, retail, DTC.
  • SMB: an owner buys through peers and integrations.
  • Enterprise and regulated: a committee, security review and procurement.
  • Government: contract vehicles.

Then the sequence: beachhead, positioning, channel, unit economics, proof of demand.

Trap: The rabbit rung (about $1k a year per customer) is too costly for zero-touch trust and too cheap to pay a salesperson; Janz found rabbits less straightforward to hunt than flies or elephants.
Trap: B2B vs B2C as the main split. A $15 widget and a $9-a-month SMB tool share a motion; a $200k hospital deal shares little with either.
Dental-office payroll at $300 a month is an SMB rung: peers, associations and practice-system integrations, not paid social or field sales.

cards.q: A product priced at $2,500 a year struggles with both ads and sales reps. Why?
cards.a: It is on Janz's rabbit rung: too expensive for self-serve trust, too cheap to fund a salesperson per deal.

cards.q: In Janz's ladder, how many $10k-a-year customers make $100M?
cards.a: About 10,000 (deer).

concepts.s: Win one narrow segment completely before expanding, because mainstream buyers buy on references from people like them.

x.b:
Geoffrey Moore (Crossing the Chasm): early adopters buy the vision; the mainstream buys references. Dominate one niche, then use it to topple adjacent ones (the bowling pin).

A good beachhead: urgent, costly pain; buyers you can name and reach; buyers who talk to each other; a whole product you can deliver, with partners if needed.
Trap: "Our market is everyone." A small budget spread wide never reaches the reference density that tips a segment.
Independent dental offices in one state, reached through the state association, before "all of healthcare".
Can you name 50 target buyers today, and where they gather?

cards.q: Two segments: one large but scattered, one small with an active trade association. Which is the better beachhead?
cards.a: The small one: reachable buyers who talk to each other create references fast.

cards.q: Why does winning one niche help win the next?
cards.a: Mainstream buyers in adjacent niches buy on references from peers in the niche you already own.

concepts.s: Positioning starts from what customers would do without you, then names your unique value, who cares most, and the category that makes it obvious.

x.b:
April Dunford's order (Obviously Awesome), each step built on the last:

  1. Competitive alternatives (often a spreadsheet, an intern, or nothing).
  2. Unique attributes.
  3. Value those attributes create.
  4. Best-fit customers.
  5. Market category.
  6. Relevant trends (optional).

The category sets who you are compared with and what price buyers expect.
Trap: Starting from features. Buyers think in alternatives, and the status quo wins many B2B deals.
"Dental practice payroll" sets a different comparison, price and channel than "HR software" for the same product.

cards.q: Your demo wins praise but deals stall at "we'll keep using Excel". Which positioning step did you skip?
cards.a: Competitive alternatives: you positioned against products instead of the status quo.

cards.q: What does choosing a market category do?
cards.a: It frames who you compete with, which features buyers expect and what price seems right.

concepts.s: Most companies win through one dominant channel, so test several cheaply and then concentrate on the one that works.

x.b:
Weinberg and Mares (Traction) list 19 channels, from SEO and content to sales, communities and engineering as marketing. Bullseye: brainstorm all 19, rank a few, test cheaply, then focus on the winner until it saturates.

  • Consumer apps: app-store search, short video, referrals, paid social.
  • Retail: brokers, distributors, buyer meetings.
  • SMB vertical: associations, conferences, integrations, advisors.
  • Enterprise: founder outbound, intros, partners.

Trap: Defaulting to the channel you already know.
Trap: Five channels at once with no budget for any: no test reaches a readable signal.
Three cheap tests for SMB payroll: one association webinar, one integration listing, 100 cold emails. Double down on whichever books demos at the lowest cost.

cards.q: You have $3k to find a channel. What does Bullseye prescribe?
cards.a: Run a few cheap parallel tests, then concentrate on the one with the best cost per qualified lead.

cards.q: Why not run every channel at modest spend?
cards.a: None gets enough volume to separate signal from noise.

concepts.s: Consumer apps live on retention first and cheap acquisition second, because paid installs only pay when a user is worth more than they cost.

x.b:
1. Ship narrow to one community; measure day 1, 7 and 30 retention by cohort.
  2. Fix retention before buying traffic; a flattening curve means a core stays.
  3. Build a loop: invites, sharing, content that ranks; a viral coefficient above 1 means growth sustains itself.
  4. Monetize to fit the use: subscriptions for utility, purchases or ads for games.
  5. Buy installs only when revenue per user beats cost per install.

Freemium converts in the low single digits; trials convert higher.

Trap: Buying installs to look like traction. Bought users who churn worsen the curve and burn cash.
Trap: Living on one platform's algorithm; reach can vanish with a policy change.
A game with 40% day-1 but 3% day-30 retention fixes onboarding and progression before any ad spend.

cards.q: Day-30 retention keeps falling toward zero. Should you start paid acquisition?
cards.a: No: fix retention first; until the curve flattens, every bought user leaks.

cards.q: What does a viral coefficient above 1 mean?
cards.a: Each user brings in more than one new user, so growth sustains itself.

concepts.s: Physical goods are a cash-and-channel game: prove demand cheaply, model contribution margin per unit, and fund the channel before it pays you.

x.b:
• Retail: brokers pitch buyers; distributors deliver; buyers cut items on velocity (units per store per week). The FTC's 2003 study found slotting fees of about $2,300-21,800 per item per retailer per metro, and suppliers estimated $1.5-2M for a national grocery launch. Walmart's Open Call takes US-made pitches through RangeMe.
  • DTC and Amazon: Amazon's referral fee is 15% in most categories, with a $0.30 minimum; first orders often lose money after ad cost, so repeat purchase carries it.
  • Hardware: pre-orders before tooling; FCC authorization for electronics; months of cash out before revenue.
Trap: Winning a big chain you can't fund: slotting, free fill, promotions and chargebacks arrive before 30-90 day payment.
Prove demand at local stores and online pre-orders, then one regional chain, then national on sales data.

cards.q: A buyer offers 500 stores. What do you check before saying yes?
cards.a: Cash to fund slotting, free fill, promotions and payment terms, and whether velocity will hold.

cards.q: Why do DTC brands obsess over repeat purchase?
cards.a: The first order often loses money after ad cost; repeat orders carry the economics.

concepts.s: Small businesses buy on peer trust, workflow fit and painless switching, so vertical tools win through industry networks and integrations while horizontal tools win through product-led adoption.

x.b:
• Vertical (one industry): the owner or office manager buys. Do one painful workflow far better, integrate with the industry's system of record, sell through associations, conferences and advisors, then expand into adjacent workflows and embedded payments.
  • Horizontal product-led: fast time to value, a defined activation event, sharing that pulls in teammates, then sales on product-qualified accounts.

Trap: Underestimating onboarding. Migrating data from the old system is the real switching cost.
Trap: Assuming product-led means no sales. Bigger accounts still need a person for security and contracts.
Dental payroll integrates with the practice management system, launches at a state dental meeting, and migrates payroll history for free.

cards.q: Trials sign up but few convert. Which product-led metric do you engineer first?
cards.a: Time to value and the activation event that predicts retention.

cards.q: How does vertical SMB software usually grow revenue per customer?
cards.a: Adding adjacent workflows and embedded payments or financial products.

concepts.s: A founder sells the first enterprise deals until the path to close is repeatable, because that path is what the first salesperson must copy.

x.b:
1. Outbound to a named list plus warm intros.
  2. Find the champion (feels the pain) and the economic buyer (owns the budget).
  3. Paid pilots with written success criteria and a path to contract.
  4. Security ready: questionnaires and, for most US buyers, a SOC 2 report.
  5. Map procurement and budget cycles early.
  6. Hire one salesperson when the path repeats, then a second to tell skill from luck.

MEDDICC (metrics, economic buyer, decision criteria and process, pain, champion, competition) checks whether a deal is real.
Trap: Free pilots with no success criteria or budget owner are unpaid consulting.
A pilot that ends in "we loved it" but has no budget line was never a deal; qualify the economic buyer before starting.

cards.q: Your champion loves the product but the deal stalls for months. What did you likely miss?
cards.a: The economic buyer: the person who owns the budget and signs.

cards.q: When should a founder hire the first salesperson?
cards.a: After closing deals personally and seeing a repeatable path to close.

concepts.s: Healthcare and government add regulation, integration and contract vehicles to enterprise selling, so compliance readiness and proof of value come before the first meeting.

x.b:
• Healthcare: handling PHI for a covered entity makes you a business associate, so you sign a BAA. Clinical, IT, compliance and finance all weigh in. The EHR is the system of record; Epic's third-party program is Showroom. Billable services ease adoption.
  • Government: SBIR/STTR awards were reauthorized in April 2026 through September 30, 2031. Agencies buy through contract vehicles such as GSA schedules, or via prime contractors. Cloud software needs FedRAMP, which is moving to its 20x process (as of Nov 2026).

Trap: Pitching clinical benefit to a buyer judged on cost. Match value to each committee member's metric.
Trap: Mistaking a program office's enthusiasm for a buying path.
Start with specialty groups or a health system's innovation team, prove one outcome in numbers, and bring the BAA and data-flow diagram to the first meeting.

cards.q: A health system loves your demo but legal won't proceed. What document is usually missing?
cards.a: A business associate agreement (BAA) for handling PHI.

cards.q: Name two routes into federal buying for a small vendor.
cards.a: Subcontract through a prime contractor, or sell through an existing contract vehicle; SBIR/STTR awards are a third, non-dilutive route.

concepts.s: A marketplace must reach liquidity in a narrow slice first, usually by seeding the harder side by hand.

x.b:
1. Constrain: one city, category or campus.
  2. Seed the harder side (usually supply) manually or with a tool useful before demand arrives.
  3. Measure liquidity: share of listings that transact or searches that match.
  4. Set a take rate the value justifies.
  5. Expand only when the first slice sustains itself.

Trap: National launch: both sides too thin to match, so both leave.
Trap: Disintermediation: repeat pairs move off-platform unless you add ongoing value (payments, insurance, scheduling).
A tutoring marketplace launches at one university with 30 hand-recruited tutors before opening a second campus.

cards.q: Buyers and sellers meet on your platform, then transact privately. What is this and what counters it?
cards.a: Disintermediation; counter with ongoing value such as payments, insurance or scheduling.

cards.q: Why constrain a new marketplace's geography or category?
cards.a: To reach liquidity in a small slice instead of thin coverage everywhere.

concepts.s: Selling a service earns cash from the first customer and reveals the market, and productizing it (fixed scope, process and price) makes it repeatable without building software yet.

x.b:
1. Sell an outcome to a niche you know, priced by value or project, not hours.
  2. Standardize: same deliverable, same process, fixed price.
  3. Template and then delegate or automate each repeated step.
  4. Use client patterns to spot software opportunities and pre-sell before building.

Fits a side launch: little capital, immediate revenue, and a list of named buyers for any product that follows.

Trap: Custom work for every client: a staffing business with founder hours as the cap.
Trap: Assuming services convert neatly into software; many stay services, which can still be good outcomes.
Fixed-price "dental payroll cleanup" for 10 practices reveals the same three failures, which become the first product's scope.

cards.q: What makes a service "productized"?
cards.a: Fixed scope, fixed process, fixed price for a standard deliverable.

cards.q: Why start with services before software on a side launch?
cards.a: Low capital, immediate revenue, and direct evidence of what buyers will pay for.

concepts.s: Price sets your rung, and the business works only when each customer's gross profit repays what it cost to win them, fast enough to fund growth.

x.b:
• CAC = sales and marketing spend (including salaries) / new customers.
  • Payback months = CAC / (monthly revenue x gross margin).
  • LTV (simple) = monthly gross profit / monthly churn; 3:1 LTV:CAC is a common rule of thumb.
  • Physical goods: contribution margin per unit after cost of goods, freight, channel margin, trade spend, returns and acquisition.

Price to value against the alternative, on a value metric that grows with the customer (seat, location, transaction).

Revenue grows only three ways: more customers, more sold to each customer, or a higher price.

Trap: Underpricing to win early customers locks you on a rung whose channel you can't afford.
Trap: Revenue instead of gross profit in payback.
CAC $1,200, $100 a month at 80% margin: payback is 15 months. Raising price to $150 cuts it to 10 without touching acquisition.

cards.q: CAC is $1,200, price $100 a month, gross margin 80%. What is the payback?
Why is a price increase often the fastest unit-economics fix?
cards.a: It raises revenue per customer without changing acquisition cost.

concepts.s: Treat only commitments as evidence: ask about past behavior, not opinions of your idea, and scale only when users would miss the product.

x.b:
The Mom Test (Rob Fitzpatrick): talk about their life, not your idea; ask about specifics in the past, not hypotheticals; talk less. Compliments, fluff and feature ideas are bad data. Each meeting should end in commitment or advancement paid in time, reputation or money.

Ladder: interviews, then deposits, letters of intent and paid pilots, then manual delivery (Paul Graham's "do things that don't scale"), then retention. Sean Ellis's test: 40%+ of users "very disappointed" without it signals product-market fit. Write kill criteria (milestone, metric, date) first.
Trap: "Would you use this?" invites a polite yes. Ask when they last had the problem and what they did.
Bad: "Would you pay for faster payroll?" Good: "Walk me through last month's payroll. What broke? What did that cost you?" Then ask for a pilot.

cards.q: A prospect says "I'd definitely buy that." How do you classify it, and what next?
cards.a: Fluff (a future promise); ask about a specific past instance, then for a commitment such as a pilot or intro.

cards.q: What does the Sean Ellis test measure, and its threshold?
cards.a: Share of users who'd be very disappointed without the product; 40% or more signals fit.
